reader.title: Wilcox tragedy, Plain City, Ohio
bases: The papers report a man who killed his wife and then died by hanging, called a suicide in the wire reports (A1, A4, A11); only one later dispatch reports a local belief that neighbors lynched him (A7), and no paper names anyone's race.

Wilcox died by hanging, but most reports call it suicide (A1, A4, A11). The Plain City dispatch of Oct. 13 reports only a neighborhood 'belief' that a party of neighbors captured and strangled him, and it says the mystery would hardly be cleared up (A7); no report names a group, a number or a confirmed killing.

Several reports agree that Wilcox fatally beat his wife and then died by hanging in a nearby wood (A1, A4, A11). They call it suicide, but the Oct. 13 Plain City dispatch reports a widespread local belief that neighbors lynched him (A7).

summary.text: The Wilcox tragedy was the killing of Mrs. Wilcox by her husband, William Wilcox, near Plain City, Ohio, on the night of October 10, 1881, followed by Wilcox's death by hanging in a nearby wood.
Wire reports called his death a suicide, but a Plain City dispatch three days later reported a growing local belief that neighbors had captured and lynched him.
Wilcox, once a well-to-do farmer from a prominent and wealthy family, had been drinking heavily for two years and had several times been accused of attacking his wife and family.

According to the Chicago Tribune, he had been jailed at Marysville for a third attempt to kill his family and was released the Saturday before, when his father, Asa Wilcox, bailed him out and took him home.
On the night of October 10 he left his father's house, saying he was going to a neighbor's, and instead went to his wife's house and cut and beat her.
He was found the next morning hanged to a tree in the woods nearby, and his wife died that day.
One brief instead said he shot his wife.
Wilcox's children refused to bury him, and his body lay uncovered in the farmhouse kitchen, bloodied from two head wounds, until a brother had it washed and placed in a burial case.

On October 13 a large crowd gathered at the home, including a score of men Wilcox had threatened, and some openly celebrated his death and proposed dragging his body behind mules or burning it on a log-pile.
Rev. Brodrick of the Plain City M. E. Church preached over both bodies at Sandy school-house, where they were buried in separate parts of the graveyard.
No report of an inquest into either death appears in the coverage.
The first wire ran under the headline "The Curse of Rum," and the Chicago Tribune headlined "A Drunkard Kills His Wife," treating the case as a temperance and domestic-crime story.

News summaries in the Daily Republican, the Lancaster Daily Intelligencer, the Savannah Morning News, the Watertown Republican and the Crawford Avalanche repeated the suicide version in a sentence or two between October 12 and 20.

The fuller October 13 dispatch, printed in the Wheeling Daily Intelligencer as "The Last Act," reported the lynching belief and called the crowd's talk "disgustingly suggestive of a vitiated and overheated condition of mind."
No report mentions the race of anyone involved.
The earliest reports said Wilcox hanged himself, and an Ohio state column a week later still said he "suicided by hanging."

The Plain City dispatch instead reported a belief that the neighbors who found the wife's body caught Wilcox trying to escape, threw him into a shallow well, and then strangled him partly suspended from a tree limb, pointing to his drenched clothing and to two or three searchers who had left the neighborhood.
The same dispatch said the mystery would "hardly be cleared up satisfactorily."

accounts.gist: Wilcox fatally injured his wife and then hanged himself in a neighboring wood; he had been released from jail days earlier.

accounts.label: Chicago Tribune account
accounts.gist: After his father bailed him out, Wilcox went to his wife's house, cut and beat her, then hanged himself to a tree in the woods, where he was found dead in the morning.

accounts.label: Plain City dispatch, Oct. 13 (neighborhood belief)
accounts.gist: Neighbors who found the wife's body and went searching for Wilcox were believed to have captured him, thrown him into a well and strangled him from a tree limb; two or three of them were absent from the neighborhood.

accounts.label: Daily Globe brief
accounts.gist: Wilcox shot and killed his wife on Tuesday and then hanged himself.

framing.detail: The first wire ran as 'The Curse of Rum,' a temperance story about the 'dissipated member of a prominent and wealthy family.'
The Chicago Tribune headlined 'A Drunkard Kills His Wife and Then Hangs Himself' and called Wilcox 'The murderer and suicide.'

'The Last Act' called Wilcox 'the murderer' and reported the lynching belief as plausible, but called the crowd's talk of dragging or burning the body 'disgustingly suggestive of a vitiated and overheated condition of mind.'
News summaries and state columns carried the suicide version only, without the lynching belief.

conflicts.note: The suicide version is the earliest and most widely carried. The lynching version is a belief reported by the later local dispatch, which itself says the mystery would hardly be cleared up; neither is confirmed by an inquest in the coverage.
The shooting version appears only in a one-line brief; the fuller reports describe a beating.

info: Wilcox assaulted his wife on the night of Monday, Oct. 10, 1881, and was found dead the next morning; Mrs. Wilcox died Oct. 11.
Plain City, Ohio; the Wilcox farm, about three miles east of town, and a nearby wood
Mrs. Wilcox, killed by her husband; William Wilcox, found hanged, by suicide or, by a local belief, by neighbors. No race is stated for either.
Wilcox was reported to have fatally beaten his wife (cut and beat her, A4; shot her, A6). He had been jailed for earlier attempts to kill his family.
Wire reports: Wilcox hanged himself. Local belief: 'a party of his neighbors' who went searching for him after the wife's body was found.
Wilcox and his wife were buried the same day, in separate parts of the Sandy school-house graveyard, after a joint service by Rev. Brodrick of the Plain City M. E. Church.
